title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
subject: ophthalmology-ent
setting: Emergency department, primary care, ENT clinic
summary: Diagnose posterior canal BPPV when the Dix-Hallpike test provokes vertigo with torsional upbeating nystagmus, and treat with the Epley manoeuvre rather than vestibular suppressants or imaging. Continuous vertigo, atypical nystagmus or any neurological sign points to a central cause: HINTS by a trained clinician and MRI, not CT.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Brief spinning vertigo, lasting seconds and usually under a minute, triggered by head movement: rolling over in bed, lying down, looking up or bending forward. No hearing loss or neurological symptoms; mild imbalance or nausea between attacks is common.
Posterior canal BPPV is the commonest form, lateral (horizontal) canal BPPV the next; anterior canal BPPV is rare.
Continuous vertigo lasting hours to days with spontaneous nystagmus, nausea and unsteadiness is an acute vestibular syndrome (vestibular neuritis or stroke), not BPPV.
Assess factors that change management: impaired mobility or balance, CNS disease, lack of home support and risk of falls, particularly in older adults.

sections.title: Positional tests
items: Dix-Hallpike: from sitting, turn the head 45 degrees to one side, then lie the patient back quickly with the neck extended about 20 degrees and that ear down. Watch the eyes for up to a minute, sit up, then test the other side.

Positive for posterior canal BPPV (strong recommendation): vertigo with torsional, upbeating nystagmus toward the lower ear, starting after a short latency and fading within about 60 seconds; it often reverses on sitting up.

If the history fits but Dix-Hallpike shows horizontal or no nystagmus, do a supine roll test: horizontal nystagmus on turning the head to each side indicates lateral canal BPPV (geotropic or apogeotropic).
Do not order imaging or vestibular function tests when the diagnostic criteria are met and there are no atypical features (AAO-HNS).

sections.title: Central red flags (think posterior circulation stroke)
items: Positional nystagmus that is purely downbeating or vertical, has no latency, does not fade, does not fit a canal pattern, or does not respond to repeated manoeuvres.
Any neurological symptom or sign: diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, limb ataxia, weakness or numbness, Horner syndrome, inability to sit or walk unaided, new severe headache or neck pain.

Acute vestibular syndrome with nystagmus: a trained clinician should use HINTS. A normal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation suggests a central cause. Also check hearing (finger rub): new unilateral hearing loss raises concern for stroke (GRACE-3).
Central or equivocal HINTS, or no trained examiner: MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging. Do not use CT to rule out stroke in dizziness (GRACE-3).
Spontaneous episodic vertigo with vascular risk factors or other ischaemic symptoms: assess for TIA and consider CT or MR angiography (GRACE-3).

sections.title: Repositioning manoeuvres
items: Posterior canal BPPV: treat, or refer to a clinician who can, with a canalith repositioning procedure such as the Epley manoeuvre (strong recommendation). Repeat if the Dix-Hallpike stays positive; the Semont manoeuvre is an alternative.

Epley for the right ear: right Dix-Hallpike position; turn the head 90 degrees to the left; roll onto the left side with the face turned 45 degrees toward the floor; then sit up. Hold each position until nystagmus and vertigo settle (about 30 to 60 seconds).
Do not impose postural restrictions (sleeping upright, collars) after the manoeuvre (strong recommendation against).
Lateral canal BPPV: barbecue (Lempert) roll or Gufoni manoeuvre by a trained clinician, or refer.
Observation with follow-up is an option because BPPV often resolves on its own; vestibular rehabilitation, self-administered or supervised, is also an option, especially for residual imbalance.

sections.title: Medicines
items: Do not routinely treat BPPV with vestibular suppressants such as antihistamines (meclizine, cinnarizine, promethazine, dimenhydrinate) or benzodiazepines: they do not resolve BPPV, can impair central compensation and increase falls.
A single antiemetic dose (for example prochlorperazine or ondansetron) may be used for severe nausea around the manoeuvre.

sections.title: Disposition and follow-up
items: Most patients go home after repositioning. Reassess within 1 month to document resolution or persistence.
Persistent symptoms: re-test for unresolved or other-canal BPPV and look for other peripheral vestibular or central disorders; refer to ENT, neurology or vestibular rehabilitation.
Educate about fall risk, the high chance of recurrence and the importance of follow-up; patients can be taught a home Epley for recurrences on the known side.

sections.title: Older adults and limited neck movement
items: Older adults: BPPV is common and often missed; ask about falls, check home support, and review sedating medicines.

Severe cervical or back disease, recent neck injury or suspected arterial dissection: avoid forceful neck extension; use modified positioning (for example a tilting couch) or refer to a vestibular specialist.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Labelling dizziness as BPPV without a positive positional test.
Applying HINTS to positional or episodic vertigo, or without spontaneous nystagmus: it is only for the acute vestibular syndrome.
Long courses of cinnarizine or prochlorperazine instead of a repositioning manoeuvre.
Being reassured by a normal CT when posterior circulation stroke is suspected.

drugs.name: Prochlorperazine
drugs.dose: 12.5 mg by deep IM injection once, or 5 to 10 mg orally up to three times daily for 1 to 2 days only
drugs.notes: Severe nausea only; not a treatment for BPPV. Sedation, extrapyramidal effects and falls in older adults.

drugs.name: Ondansetron
drugs.dose: 4 mg IV or orally, single dose
drugs.notes: Alternative antiemetic around manoeuvres; caution with QT prolongation.
